The Crossing of the Red Sea

Nicolas Poussin, 1633–1634
National Gallery of Victoria, Melbourne

Created 1633–1634; depicts The Exodus, traditionally placed in the Late Bronze Age. This is artistic depiction, not archaeological evidence of the event.

Poussin stages the sea crossing as a composed classical drama. Egyptian armor, drapery, and landscape belong to seventeenth-century European painting, not to New Kingdom Egypt.

“I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will crush your head.”

— GENESIS 3:15
SUMMARY

In Eden's perfection, Adam and Eve choose rebellion over relationship, eating the forbidden fruit. Shame enters the world as they hide from God. Yet even in judgment, God promises a descendant who will crush the serpent and restore what was lost.

WORLD AROUND THIS MOMENT
Eastern Nile frontier / northern Sinai waters

The crossing — body of water unidentified

The story pins a people between chariot power and water. Geography here is a constraint: Egypt's military roads ran the northern Sinai; wetlands and lakes sat on the eastern edge of the Delta. The biblical text gives a deliverance at the sea. It does not give a modern grid reference. Later paintings, including the one this journey may show, are reception — how Europe imagined the scene centuries afterward — not evidence of a particular beach.

HOW PEOPLE MOVE
SCHOLARLY INFERENCE
Egyptian military and trade routes crossed northern Sinai. A fleeing group would have had to leave the Nile corridor; which water they met is not settled.
WHAT SURVIVES
DISPUTED
Proposed identifications (Bitter Lakes, Lake Sirbonis, Gulf of Suez, Gulf of Aqaba) remain competing scholarly reconstructions. None is archaeologically tagged as the crossing.

WHAT CHANGED
The narrative leaves the irrigated imperial center for a threshold landscape — water, wind, and an army's reach — without a verified campsite.

UNCERTAIN
Route, body of water, and date are all disputed. The camera is a storytelling choice. It is not a survey peg.

CHRONOLOGY
The Hebrew yam suf is traditionally rendered Red Sea; many scholars read a reed sea or lagoon on the eastern Delta. The map must choose a shore. That choice is not a verified waypoint.

DISPUTED
SCHOLARLY INFERENCE
SOURCES (2)
DEVOTIONAL REFLECTION

Your shame and hiding can't separate you from God—He pursues you even in your failure with a rescue plan.

THE WORLD OF JONAH

Nineveh

Opposite Mosul · Tigris valley

The city in the story belongs to a wider world of palaces, conquest, gardens, and books written in clay.

Nineveh stood beside the Tigris, opposite modern Mosul in northern Iraq. The marker locates the ancient city, not Jonah’s movements within it.

A city across time
Early seventh century BCE
An imperial capital

Sennacherib transforms Nineveh into a major Assyrian capital. Palace reliefs display royal building projects and conquest.

Seventh century BCE
A library in clay

Ashurbanipal’s library brings together cuneiform texts. More than 30,000 tablets and fragments have been found in Nineveh’s ruins.

612 BCE
The capital falls

A Babylonian–Median coalition captures Nineveh. The clay tablets preserve traces of its intellectual life.

A flood story, pressed into clay

This is the city’s history, not a date for Jonah’s visit. The book does not name its king; its relationship to these events remains uncertain.

ARTISTIC DEPICTION
NOT ARCHAEOLOGICAL EVIDENCE
The Crossing of the Red Sea

Nicolas Poussin, 1633–1634
National Gallery of Victoria, Melbourne

Created 1633–1634; depicts The Exodus, traditionally placed in the Late Bronze Age. This is artistic depiction, not archaeological evidence of the event.

Poussin stages the sea crossing as a composed classical drama. Egyptian armor, drapery, and landscape belong to seventeenth-century European painting, not to New Kingdom Egypt.

Source record
PD-Art
Nicolas Poussin, The Crossing of the Red Sea, 1633–1634, National Gallery of Victoria. Public domain.
The sea
1446 BC
·
DELIVERANCE
·
JOURNEY
LISTEN
VOLUME

“I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will crush your head.”

— GENESIS 3:15
SUMMARY

In Eden's perfection, Adam and Eve choose rebellion over relationship, eating the forbidden fruit. Shame enters the world as they hide from God. Yet even in judgment, God promises a descendant who will crush the serpent and restore what was lost.

WORLD AROUND THIS MOMENT
Eastern Nile frontier / northern Sinai waters

The crossing — body of water unidentified

The story pins a people between chariot power and water. Geography here is a constraint: Egypt's military roads ran the northern Sinai; wetlands and lakes sat on the eastern edge of the Delta. The biblical text gives a deliverance at the sea. It does not give a modern grid reference. Later paintings, including the one this journey may show, are reception — how Europe imagined the scene centuries afterward — not evidence of a particular beach.

HOW PEOPLE MOVE
SCHOLARLY INFERENCE
Egyptian military and trade routes crossed northern Sinai. A fleeing group would have had to leave the Nile corridor; which water they met is not settled.
WHAT SURVIVES
DISPUTED
Proposed identifications (Bitter Lakes, Lake Sirbonis, Gulf of Suez, Gulf of Aqaba) remain competing scholarly reconstructions. None is archaeologically tagged as the crossing.

WHAT CHANGED
The narrative leaves the irrigated imperial center for a threshold landscape — water, wind, and an army's reach — without a verified campsite.

UNCERTAIN
Route, body of water, and date are all disputed. The camera is a storytelling choice. It is not a survey peg.

CHRONOLOGY
The Hebrew yam suf is traditionally rendered Red Sea; many scholars read a reed sea or lagoon on the eastern Delta. The map must choose a shore. That choice is not a verified waypoint.

DISPUTED
SCHOLARLY INFERENCE
SOURCES (2)
DEVOTIONAL REFLECTION

Your shame and hiding can't separate you from God—He pursues you even in your failure with a rescue plan.
